- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) and forecast is trending upward, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) and forecast is trending downward, increase forecast slope to avoid premature pessimism.  
- When history shows recent sharp spikes followed by rapid decline, model should not overcorrect — maintain slight lag in downward adjustment.  
- If forecast mean is significantly above true mean (e.g., >10% over 30d), apply mean reversion bias toward historical median or 14-day moving average.  
- For 30d forecasts with strong sentiment reversal (e.g., from +0.67 to 0.00), model should not assume immediate continuation — add 2–3 day lag in price correction.  
- If forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows sharp drop, reduce forecast by 5–10% in first 5–7 days of forecast horizon.  
- When sentiment is high but price drops sharply, model should not assume sentiment will persist — add 1–2 day buffer for sentiment decay.
